title: Economies of ale: pubs in the time of COVID-19
meta_description: Pubs were among those businesses forced to close during  restrictions introduced to halt the spread of the coronavirus (COVID-19).  In their own words, landlords shared their experiences of the effect of lockdown on their businesses.

body.h2: Pub landlords' “high confidence” about their future business survival has peaked above 20% for the first time
body.text: Pubs and bars were among the thousands of non-essential businesses told to close since the [first coronavirus lockdown in March 2020](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-52012432). At that time there were 38,870 pubs and bars in the UK employing 467,000 people.

body.h2: Pub landlords' “high confidence” about their future business survival has peaked above 20% for the first time
body.text: While funding schemes have been introduced by the government to help keep these businesses alive until they are able to resume trading fully, the [series of lockdown measures](https://www.instituteforgovernment.org.uk/sites/default/files/timeline-lockdown-web.pdf) have resulted in the establishments shutting up shop for months at a time.

body.h2: Pub landlords' “high confidence” about their future business survival has peaked above 20% for the first time
body.text: For this article, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) is using the results of the [Business Insights and Conditions Survey (BICS)](https://www.ons.gov.uk/businessindustryandtrade/business/businessservices/articles/insightsofthebusinessimpactofcoronaviruscovid19survey/24august2020to4april2021) from October 2020 onwards, which shows that in October 2020, just 6% of landlords had “high confidence” that their establishments would survive beyond three months. By early February 2021, the proportion of “high confidence” had dropped to its lowest recorded level of 1%.

body.h2: Furlough scheme has been vital for pub staff
body.text: Furlough scheme has been vital for pub staff

body.h2: Furlough scheme has been vital for pub staff
body.text: Prior to the pandemic, employment in pubs and bars (particularly pub chains) was increasing, as we showed in our previous [Economies of ale article](https://www.ons.gov.uk/businessindustryandtrade/business/activitysizeandlocation/articles/economiesofalesmallpubscloseaschainsfocusonbigbars/changesintheukpubsandbarssector2001to2019). Given the interruptions to trade in 2020, it’s likely that staffing levels will have changed significantly. [Wider reports from those representing the hospitality industries](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-54435065) suggest jobs may have been lost during the pandemic, with workers retraining for other industries.

body.h2: Furlough scheme has been vital for pub staff
body.text: The government’s [HM Revenue and Customs Coronavirus Job Retention Scheme (CJRS)](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/claim-for-wages-through-the-coronavirus-job-retention-scheme), also known as furlough, has been an important means of business support during the pandemic. It has enabled landlords to keep staff on their books while their establishments have been closed.

body.h2: Furlough scheme has been vital for pub staff
body.text: While the furlough scheme has been a means of survival, it’s pointless if they have no job to come back to. Pub and bar owners, November 2020

body.h2: Furlough scheme has been vital for pub staff
body.text: While the furlough scheme has been a means of survival, it’s pointless if they have no job to come back to.

body.h2: Furlough scheme has been vital for pub staff
body.text: At its peak in the November 2020 lockdown, 91% of pub and bar staff were on furlough. This number has now decreased to 55%.

body.h2: Furlough scheme has been vital for pub staff
body.text: This compares with overall 8% to 15% of staff on furlough in all other businesses during the same period, indicating the heavier reliance of pubs and bars on the scheme.

body.h2: Furlough scheme has been vital for pub staff
body.text: We can increasingly see a downward trend of pub and bar staff on furlough since restrictions were lifted on beer gardens. Despite this, the percentage of staff that were on furlough has remained high. This suggests that where pubs and bars have been open, they have been operating with minimal staff.

body.h2: Furlough scheme has been vital for pub staff
body.h4: The percentage of the workforce on furlough in pub and bar businesses is considerably higher than that of all other businesses
body.text: Not all pub and bar jobs will have been saved by the furlough scheme. In the weeks just after Christmas 2020, 12% of pubs and bars reported that it was likely they would make redundancies in the next three months. This number fell to approximately 4% by late February 2021. It is unclear whether this is because of increased certainty or because the redundancies had already gone through.

body.text: Run up to Christmas was financially difficult for pubs

body.h2: Run up to Christmas was financially difficult for pubs
body.text: The weeks leading up to Christmas are normally busy for pubs and bars, but December 2020 saw huge losses in trade.

body.h2: Run up to Christmas was financially difficult for pubs
body.text: Missing out on Christmas trade has been detrimental. Pub and bar owners, December 2020

body.h2: Run up to Christmas was financially difficult for pubs

body.h2: Run up to Christmas was financially difficult for pubs
body.text: The [tier system](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/full-list-of-local-restriction-tiers-by-area), introduced on 2 December 2020, placed areas of England under specific sets of restrictions. Pubs and bars in areas placed under tier 3 and 4, the strictest of conditions, had to close. The tier system was replaced in England on 4 January 2021 by another [national lockdown](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/prime-minister-announces-national-lockdown).

body.h2: Run up to Christmas was financially difficult for pubs
body.text: By mid-December 2020, more than 80% of pubs and bars recorded that their profits were more than 50% below what they would normally expect for the time of year, with that number soaring to 100% by late December 2020.

However, those losses have recently started to decrease, with around 33% of pubs recording significant profit losses, because restrictions have eased since mid-April.

This will be explored further in our upcoming publication on the hospitality sector, due to publish in July 2021.

body.h2: About the data
body.text: About the data

body.h2: About the data
body.text: The indicators and analysis presented in this article are based on responses from the Business Insights and Conditions Survey (BICS).

body.h2: About the data
body.text: BICS is a voluntary, fortnightly survey that captures businesses' responses on how their financial performance, workforce, prices, trade, and business resilience have been affected, over a two-week reference period.

body.h2: About the data
body.text: Because of a lack of imputed data, these estimates may differ from published estimates. A detailed description of the weighting methodology can be found in the recently published [Quality and Methodology information report](https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/economicoutputandproductivity/output/methodologies/businessinsightsandconditionssurveybicsqmi).

body.h2: About the data
body.text: BICS responses were sifted by their Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) Code. SIC Code "56302: Public houses and bars" is used to capture "Pubs" and any other respondent is classified under "All other businesses".

body.h2: About the data
body.text: The quotes used in the article are derived from the free-text responses within BICS. Sentiment analysis has been carried out and the responses have been summarised and rephrased to safeguard the anonymity of the respondents.
